results.proposed_proof:
**Given:** The finite sectional mass identity and the product-kernel pre-gelation solution.

[F1] [[thm-finite-sectional-positivity-and-mass-reservoir-conservation]]: finite sectional event dynamics conserve retained-plus-reservoir mass exactly.

[F2] [[thm-product-kernel-pre-gelation-second-moment-blowup]]: for the product kernel, $M_1(t)=1$ and $M_2(t)=1/(1-t)$ on $0\le t<1$.



1.1 On a grid with top pivot $N$, the state with $n_N=1/N$ and all other retained coordinates zero has first moment $N(1/N)=1$ and second moment $N^2(1/N)=N$. Its reservoir may be zero, so the conserved augmented mass is $1$. As $N$ increases these admissible mass-one states have unbounded second moment, proving the finite mass identity alone gives no cutoff-independent moment bound. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The continuum product-kernel solution in [F2] has $M_2(t)=1/(1-t)$, which diverges at the finite time $1$ while its first moment remains $1$. The kernel $K(x,y)=xy$ is superlinear and unbounded, outside the bounded-kernel global theorem's hypotheses; therefore this example warns against inferring continuum mass-conserving global moment control from finite-grid conservation. [given, F2, algebra] ∎



Laurençot's full-text lecture notes separately state a post-gel mass-loss theorem for nontrivial weak solutions with $K(x,y)\ge\kappa(xy)^{\lambda/2}$, $\lambda\in(1,2]$, under the solution hypotheses there (Theorem 3.13, §3.3); that source result is contextual and is not used to prove the pre-gelation formula here. Kumar's dissertation reports fixed-pivot moment deviations from analytical product-kernel comparisons near gelation in its numerical examples (Chapter 3, §3.2.2); this is a numerical warning, not a substitute for the local proof above. ([Laurençot, §§3.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1801.08312); [Kumar, Chapter 3](https://www.iitrpr.ac.in/jkumar/pub/Kumar_Dissertation_web.pdf))

**Given:** The successful nearby-factorization relation, exact values $s_i=\sigma_i(\widehat B)$, and either exact readout $\widehat\sigma_i=s_i$ or the specified rounded diagonal-modulus readout.

[F1] [[thm-bidiagonal-svd-backward-error-under-local-stability]] supplies $C+E=\widehat U\begin{bmatrix}\widehat B\\0\end{bmatrix}\widehat V^*$ under its local arithmetic hypotheses, with the same tall-orientation dimensions.

[F2] [[lem-singular-values-lipschitz-in-spectral-norm]] bounds each singular-value change by the spectral norm of the matrix perturbation.

[F3] [[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]]: unitary factors preserve singular values and $\|E\|_2\le\|E\|_F$.

[F4] [[thm-singular-value-decomposition]]: taking the adjoint of an SVD interchanges its two orthonormal singular-vector bases and leaves the $p$ ordered singular values unchanged.

[F5] [[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]] supplies the successful real square-root and component-operation relative model.



1.1 By [F1], $C+E=\widehat U\begin{bmatrix}\widehat B\\0\end{bmatrix}\widehat V^*$. The tall matrix $\begin{bmatrix}\widehat B\\0\end{bmatrix}$ has the singular values of $\widehat B$, since its adjoint times itself is $\widehat B^*\widehat B$; unitary invariance in [F3] therefore gives the ordered singular values $s_i$ for $C+E$. By [F4], $C$ and $A$ have the same $p$ singular values. [F1, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F2] to $C$ and $C+E$. It gives $|\sigma_i(C+E)-\sigma_i(C)|\le\|E\|_2$; step 1.1 identifies these singular values with $s_i$ and $\sigma_i(A)$, respectively, and [F3] gives $\|E\|_2\le\|E\|_F$. [step 1.1, F2, F3, algebra]

3.1 A scaled modulus of two real components has relative norm factors between $(1-u)^4$ and $(1+u)^4$, by expanding the two scaling operations, square products and sum, square root and rescaling. Hence each rounded magnitude differs from $|d_i|$ by at most $\epsilon_{\rm read}$. If two finite lists differ coordinatewise by at most $\epsilon$, their ordered lists do too: otherwise at the violating rank the count of entries above or below the corresponding threshold contradicts the coordinatewise bounds. Apply this to the diagonal magnitudes and combine with step 2.1. For exact readout $\widehat\sigma_i=s_i$ the first bound follows already from step 2.1; for rounded readout the additional modulus allowance gives the stated extension. Real sign removal is exact. [F5, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The best-iterate and weighted-average bound [[thm-projected-subgradient-best-and-average-bound]].

[F1] The bound is $[R^2+G^2\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k^2]/(2\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k)$ ([[thm-projected-subgradient-best-and-average-bound]]).

[F2] The Euclidean norm is definite, so $\|v\|_2=0$ implies $v=0$ ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]).

[F3] The algorithm's best observed list includes $x_0$, and $g_0\in\partial f(x_0)$ on a successful first call ([[alg-projected-subgradient-method]], [[lem-projected-subgradient-finite-budget-returns-status]], [[def-subgradient-and-subdifferential]]).

[F4] For a constant real $a$, $\sum_{k<N}a=Na$ by the scaling law for finite sums ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).



1.1 For $R,G>0$, [F4] gives $\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k=N\,R/(G\sqrt N)=R\sqrt N/G$ and $G^2\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k^2=N\,R^2/N=R^2$. Substituting these values into [F1] gives $(2R^2)/(2R\sqrt N/G)=RG/\sqrt N$. [F1, F4, given, algebra]

1.2 If $R=0$, then $\|x_0-x^*\|_2=0$ and [F2] gives $x_0=x^*$; by [F3] the best observed list includes this optimizer, so its gap is zero. [given, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 If $G=0$, the successful first call satisfies $\|g_0\|_2\le0$, so [F2] gives $g_0=0$. Then $g_0\in\partial f(x_0)$ and the subgradient inequality gives $f(y)\ge f(x_0)$ for every feasible $y$; hence $x_0$ is a global minimizer and the best-iterate gap is zero. These boundary cases require no zero stepsize. [given, F2, F3, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The finite-volume shift update and cutoff-tail bound.

[F1] [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]]: with zero mortality and fertility, the exact characteristic solution is $n(t,a)=e^{-(a-t)}\mathbf1_{a\ge t}$.

[F2] [[alg-age-structured-renewal-upwind-finite-volume]]: when $\lambda=1$ and $\mu=0$, each cell mass shifts one cell to the right per step and the last-cell flux is discarded as outflow.

[F3] [[thm-age-structured-renewal-cutoff-tail-and-outflow-bound]]: for $A>T$, the initial tail above $A-T$ bounds the finite-cutoff error separately from discretization.

1.1 The exact solution in [F1] has total mass $\int_t^\infty e^{-(a-t)}da=1$ at every $t$. The exact initial cell masses are $M_j^0=e^{-(j-1)}-e^{-j}$ for $1\le j\le4$. [F1, algebra]

2.1 Since $\lambda=1$ and $\mu=0$, [F2] gives $M_1^{k+1}=0$ and $M_j^{k+1}=M_{j-1}^k$ for $2\le j\le4$. After $k$ steps, the retained total is $\sum_{j=1}^{4-k}M_j^0=1-e^{-(4-k)}$, so the error from total mass $1$ is $e^{-(4-k)}$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For $T=k=1,2,3$, the errors are respectively $e^{-3},e^{-2},e^{-1}$. The cumulative outflow is $\sum_{r=0}^{k-1}M_{4-r}^0=e^{-(4-k)}-e^{-4}$, and the initial mass omitted above $A$ is $e^{-4}$. Their sum equals the exact tail $\int_{4-k}^\infty e^{-a}da=e^{-(4-k)}$ in [F3]. The larger error at the longer horizon is the age-cutoff tail, not a time-discretization defect. [F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The finite fragmentation event convention with daughter counts $b_5(2)=b_5(3)=1$ and all other $b_5(k)=0$.

[F1] [[def-finite-discrete-coagulation-fragmentation-system]]: one fragmentation event has increment $-e_i+\sum_{k<i}b_i(k)e_k$ and requires $\sum_{k<i}k b_i(k)=i$.

[F2] [[lem-finite-coagulation-fragmentation-event-moments]]: a fragmentation event changes number by $\sum b_i(k)-1$ and mass by zero.



1.1 The daughter mass sum is $2a+3a=5a$, so this daughter law satisfies the required parent-mass normalization in [F1]. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Its number increment is $1+1-1=1$. Its mass increment is $-5a+2a+3a=0$, agreeing with [F2]. [given, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The weak formulation for a positive solution and the choices $\varphi=1,x$.

[F1] [[def-continuous-size-coagulation-fragmentation-weak-model]]: coagulation has ordered-pair factor $1/2$, while fragmentation vanishes when $\beta=0$.



1.1 With $\varphi(x)=x$, the coagulation increment is $(x+y)-x-y=0$. The integral equation therefore gives $M_1(\mu_t)=M$ on the solution interval. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 With $\varphi=1$, the increment is $1-1-1=-1$, so $N'(t)=-\kappa N(t)^2/2$. If $N_0>0$, differentiating $1/N(t)$ gives $(1/N)'=\kappa/2$ and hence the displayed formula. If $N_0=0$, positivity gives $N(t)\ge0$ and the differential equation gives $N'(t)\le0$, so $N(t)=0$, again the formula. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The data above, the characteristic renewal formula and the upwind mass update.

[F1] [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]]: the inflow is $B(t)=\int_0^\infty\beta(a)n(t,a)\,da$ and the initial datum is specified as an $L^1$ function; this example separately uses its right-hand trace at age zero.

[F2] [[thm-age-structured-renewal-characteristic-solution]]: the old cohort contributes $G(t)=\int_0^\infty\beta(x+t)S(x,t)n_0(x)\,dx$ to the Volterra birth equation.

[F3] [[alg-age-structured-renewal-upwind-finite-volume]]: $M_j^{k+1}=M_j^k-\Delta t(F_j^k-F_{j-1}^k)-\Delta t\mu_jM_j^k$ with $F_0=B_h$ and $F_j=M_j/\Delta a$.

[F4] [[thm-age-structured-renewal-upwind-positivity-mass-bound-and-stability]]: if $\Delta t/\Delta a+\Delta t\mu_\infty\le1$, the updated masses remain nonnegative.

1.1 The triangle has base length $1$ and height $1$, so $B(0)=\int_1^2\beta(a)\,da=1/2$. The chosen initial density has right-hand trace $n_0(0+)=0$, which differs from $B(0)$; hence smooth renewal-corner compatibility fails. The example uses the characteristic/weak formulation rather than assuming that compatibility. [F1, algebra]

1.2 Here $S(x,t)=e^{-t}$, so [F2] gives $G(t)=e^{-t}\int_1^2\beta(x+t)\,dx$ and $B(t)=G(t)+\int_0^t\beta(a)e^{-a}B(t-a)\,da$. The first formula records the initially present age cohort; the second is the renewal feedback term. [F2, algebra]

1.3 Use cells $[0,1],[1,2],[2,3],[3,4]$, each of width $1$, and initial masses $(0,1,0,0)$. Four-panel composite midpoint quadrature on the second cell samples fertility values $1/4,3/4,3/4,1/4$, so $B_h^0=(1/4)(1/4+3/4+3/4+1/4)=1/2$. [F1, construct, algebra]

2.1 With $\lambda=\Delta t/\Delta a=1/4$ and $\mu_j\Delta t=1/4$, the CFL sum is $1/2$. The fluxes are $F_0=1/2,F_1=0,F_2=1,F_3=0,F_4=0$, so the first updated mass vector is $(1/8,1/2,1/4,0)$. Every entry is nonnegative, in agreement with [F4]. [F3, F4, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

**Given:** A finite sectional grid containing pivots $2,3,4$ and the reported-overflow rule.

[F1] [[alg-finite-sectional-coagulation-fragmentation-balance]]: when $x_i+x_j>R$, both parents are removed and the sum of their masses is added to $L$.

[F2] [[thm-finite-sectional-positivity-and-mass-reservoir-conservation]]: each overflow event has zero augmented-mass change.



1.1 For masses $2$ and $3$, their sum is $5$, which exceeds $R=4$. The rule [F1] therefore consumes masses $2+3$ and increments the reservoir by $5$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The retained mass change is $-(2+3)=-5$ and the reservoir change is $+5$, so augmented mass change is zero, as asserted in [F2]. This reservoir entry has no later fragmentation dynamics under [F1]. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The fixed-pivot rule on a grid containing adjacent nodes $2$ and $4$.

[F1] [[def-conservative-fixed-pivot-redistribution]]: at $z\in[x_i,x_{i+1}]$, the pivot weights are $(x_{i+1}-z)/(x_{i+1}-x_i)$ and $(z-x_i)/(x_{i+1}-x_i)$.

[F2] [[lem-fixed-pivot-barycentric-identities]]: the weights sum to one and reproduce first moment $z$.



1.1 Substituting $x_i=2$, $x_{i+1}=4$, and $z=3$ in [F1] gives both weights equal to $(4-3)/(4-2)=1/2$. Thus the replacement is exactly $\tfrac12\delta_2+\tfrac12\delta_4$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The weights sum to $1$, their weighted mass is $(2+4)/2=3$, and their weighted second moment is $(2^2+4^2)/2=10$. Hence the number and mass statements agree with [F2], and the second-moment excess is $10-3^2=1$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The size-structured model, finite-volume update and exact discrete moment identities.

[F1] [[def-size-structured-transport-and-division-kernel]]: $K_y$ records daughter production and $\gamma$ records removal of the dividing parent.

[F2] [[alg-size-structured-finite-volume-flux-and-kernel-quadrature]]: the mass update uses upwind flux, loss $\mu+\gamma$ and nonnegative kernel coefficients.

[F3] [[thm-size-structured-positivity-number-and-weighted-moment-identities]]: the number and center-weighted-size balances include flux, total loss and kernel zeroth/first moments.

1.1 The parent center $2$ lies in the third cell and its daughters have size $1$, exactly the second cell center. Thus the positive midpoint kernel quadrature gives $A_{2,3}=2$ and all other daughter coefficients for the occupied parent column vanish. The CFL number is $0.1(0.1/0.5+1)=0.12$ in cell 1 and $0.1(0.1/1+1)=0.11$ in each of cells 2–4, so the global maximum is $0.12\le1$. [F1, F2, construct, algebra]

2.1 The rightward internal flux from cell $C_3$ into $C_4$ is $F_3=gM_3/h_3=0.3$; the absorbing boundary flux is $F_4=0$. The daughter source is $\Delta t A_{2,3}M_3=0.6$, and parent removal is $\Delta t\gamma M_3=0.3$. Therefore the updated cell masses are $M_2'=0.6$, $M_3'=3-0.03-0.3=2.67$, and $M_4'=0.03$, with $M_1'=0$; they are all nonnegative. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The discrete number changes from $3$ to $0.6+2.67+0.03=3.3$, an increase $0.3$ equal to $\Delta t(2-1)\gamma M_3$. The weighted-size total changes from $2\cdot3=6$ to $1\cdot0.6+2\cdot2.67+3\cdot0.03=6.03$. Formula [F3] gives the same $0.03$ increase from transport, while division contributes $\Delta t(2\cdot1-2\cdot1)M_3=0$. Thus the first moment is conserved by division and changes only by the size-growth flux in this step. [F1, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** A square linear residual with an invertible state Jacobian and a scalar objective.

[F1] [[thm-implicit-differentiation-forward-and-adjoint-formulas]]: if $R_z$ is nonsingular, the branch derivative is $-R_z^{-1}R_\theta$ and the objective gradient can be computed from $R_z^T\lambda=J_z^T$ as $J_\theta-\lambda^TR_\theta$.

[F2] [[lem-certified-linear-solve-jacobian-and-pullback-error]] supplies the certified fixed-map derivative discrepancy from inverse defects and primal residuals.



**Proof technique:** direct solve and adjoint substitution.

1.1 The system gives $u_2=1$ and $u_1+\theta u_2=2$, hence $u(\theta)=(2-\theta,1)^T$ and $J(\theta)=3-\theta$. Therefore $J'(0)=-1$. [given, algebra]

2.1 Write $R(u,\theta)=A(\theta)u-b$. At $\theta=0$, $u=(2,1)^T$, $R_u=A(0)=I$, $R_\theta=A_\theta u=(1,0)^T$, and $J_u=(1,1)$. The adjoint equation $R_u^T\lambda=J_u^T$ gives $\lambda=(1,1)^T$. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The objective has no explicit $\theta$ dependence, so $J_\theta=0$; the adjoint formula gives $J_\theta-\lambda^TR_\theta=-(1,1)\cdot(1,0)=-1$. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The adjoint result agrees with the direct derivative in step 1.1, verifying this nonsingular linear-solve instance. [step 1.1, step 3.1]

5.1 In any arithmetic satisfying the operationwise model and representing $0,1,2,3$, with these small operations in range, at $\theta=0$ the primal and basis solves give $\widehat x=(2,1)^T$ and $B=I$ exactly. Their inverse defect and primal residual are zero. The certified solve-Jacobian result [[lem-certified-linear-solve-jacobian-and-pullback-error]] therefore gives zero fixed-map discrepancy; the actual dot and product operations here are also exact, and return derivative $-1$. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The renewal characteristic/Volterra representation and the kernel and birth-history functions defined above.

[F1] [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]]: mortality survival for duration $a$ under constant rate $m$ is $e^{-ma}$.

[F2] [[thm-age-structured-renewal-characteristic-solution]]: the birth rate satisfies a Volterra equation whose renewal convolution is $\int_0^t\beta(a)S(0,a)B(t-a)\,da$.

1.1 Direct integration gives $\int\rho_\varepsilon(a)\,da=1$ and symmetry about $a_*$ gives $\int a\rho_\varepsilon(a)\,da=a_*$. Its second centered moment is $\int(a-a_*)^2\rho_\varepsilon(a)\,da=\varepsilon^2/6$. [given, algebra]

2.1 Let $b$ be Lipschitz on $[0,T]$ and take $t\ge a_*+\varepsilon$. The support of $\rho_\varepsilon$ is contained in $[0,t]$, so the convolution in [F2] is $H_\varepsilon(t)=R\int\rho_\varepsilon(a)e^{-ma}b(t-a)\,da$. For each supported $a$, $|e^{-ma}b(t-a)-e^{-ma_*}b(t-a_*)|\le(\operatorname{Lip}(b)+m\|b\|_\infty)|a-a_*|$. Since $|a-a_*|\le\varepsilon$ and the kernel has unit mass, $|H_\varepsilon(t)-Re^{-ma_*}b(t-a_*)|\le R\varepsilon(\operatorname{Lip}(b)+m\|b\|_\infty)$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 A finite-width fertility is not an exact delay: set $m=0$ and $b(s)=s^2$ on the relevant nonnegative interval. By step 1.1, $H_\varepsilon(t)=R((t-a_*)^2+\varepsilon^2/6)$, while the point-delay term is $Rb(t-a_*)=R(t-a_*)^2$; their difference is $R\varepsilon^2/6>0$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** AC; a filtered probability space whose filtration satisfies the usual conditions; and a standard two-dimensional Brownian motion $W=(W^1,W^2)$ adapted to that filtration such that $W_t-W_s$ is independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and has its standard two-dimensional normal law with covariance $(t-s)I_2$ for every $0\le s<t$ (for example, the usual augmentation of the joint natural filtration of $(W^1,W^2)$), as required by [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]; a step length $h>0$; and the It\^o integrals in the Definition.

[F1] [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]: Brownian coordinates are independent and increments after time zero are normal with their stated variances.

[F2] [[def-milstein-scheme-and-iterated-integrals]]: $L_i\sigma_j=D\sigma_j\,\sigma_i$ and $I_{ij}=\int_0^hW_s^i dW_s^j$.

[L1] [[lem-iterated-brownian-integral-identities]]: $I_{12}+I_{21}=\Delta W^1\Delta W^2$.

[F3] [[thm-ito-isometry-and-linearity-in-predictable-l2]]: $\mathbb E I_{12}^2=\mathbb E\int_0^h(W_s^1)^2ds$.

[F4] [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]: Brownian increments have Gaussian densities, and independent coordinates have product law.

[F5] [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]: conditional expectation is characterized by integrals on events in the conditioning sigma algebra.

[F6] [[thm-basic-algebra-and-order-properties-of-conditional-expectation]]: conditional expectation is linear, preserves expectation, and is $L^1$-contractive.

[F7] [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]]: $\mathbb E|Z|\le(\mathbb E|Z|^2)^{1/2}$ for square-integrable $Z$.

[F8] [[thm-conditional-expectation-is-the-l2-orthogonal-projection]]: for $I\in L^2$ and $J=\mathbb E[I\mid\mathcal G]$, $\mathbb E[(I-J)Z]=0$ for every $Z\in L^2(\mathcal G)$, in particular $Z=J$.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC is inherited through [F1], [F3], and the conditional-expectation interface [F6].



**Given:** The assumptions above.

1.1 The Jacobian of $\sigma_2$ sends $(1,0)$ to $(0,1)$, so $L_1\sigma_2=(0,1)$; the Jacobian of the constant field $\sigma_1$ is zero, so $L_2\sigma_1=(0,0)$. Thus commutativity fails. Starting from $X_0=(0,0)$, the first coordinate is $W_t^1$ and the second is $\int_0^tW_s^1dW_s^2$. The general Milstein Taylor update [F2] therefore has second-coordinate increment $I_{12}$ on the first step. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

1.2 By [L1], the endpoints determine $I_{12}+I_{21}=UV$, where $U=\Delta W^1$ and $V=\Delta W^2$. Let $\pi_n=\{0=s_0<\cdots<s_{q_n}=h\}$ be deterministic partitions with mesh $|\pi_n|\to0$, and put $S_n=\sum_{k=0}^{q_n-1}W^1_{s_k}(W^2_{s_{k+1}}-W^2_{s_k})$. The It\^o isometry [F3] gives $\mathbb E|S_n-I_{12}|^2=\sum_k\int_{s_k}^{s_{k+1}}(s-s_k)ds\le h|\pi_n|/2\to0$. [F3, L1, given]

1.3 For $0<s<h$, write $A=W_s^1$ and $U-A=W_h^1-W_s^1$; their joint density is $p_s(a)p_{h-s}(u-a)$, where $p_r$ is the $N(0,r)$ density. Dividing by the marginal density $p_h(u)$ and completing the square gives $\mathbb E[A\mid U=u]=(s/h)u$. At $s=0$ and $s=h$ the same formula follows from $A=0$ and $A=U$, respectively. For $\ell_k=s_{k+1}-s_k$, the pair $B_k=W^2_{s_{k+1}}-W^2_{s_k}$ and $V-B_k$ has density $p_{\ell_k}(b)p_{h-\ell_k}(v-b)$ when $\ell_k<h$; completing the square gives $\mathbb E[B_k\mid V=v]=(\ell_k/h)v$, and if $\ell_k=h$ then $B_k=V$ gives the same result. Independence of the two Brownian coordinate processes [F1] makes the joint density of $(A,U,B_k,V)$ the product of these two pair densities. Dividing by $p_h(u)p_h(v)$ shows that the conditional density of $(A,B_k)$ given $(U,V)=(u,v)$ factors, so $\mathbb E[AB_k\mid U,V]=(s/h)U(\ell_k/h)V$. Therefore
$$\mathbb E[S_n\mid\sigma(U,V)]=\frac{UV}{h^2}\sum_k s_k(s_{k+1}-s_k)\longrightarrow\frac{UV}{2},$$
because the sum is a left Riemann sum for $\int_0^h s\,ds=h^2/2$. By [F7], step 1.2 implies $S_n\to I_{12}$ in $L^1$; conditional expectation is $L^1$-contractive by [F6], so [F5] gives $\mathbb E[I_{12}\mid\sigma(U,V)]=UV/2$. [F1, F5, F6, F7, step 1.2, algebra]

2.1 The isometry [F3] gives $\mathbb E I_{12}^2=\int_0^h\mathbb E(W_s^1)^2ds=h^2/2$. Also $U,V$ are independent with second moments $h$, so step 1.3 gives $J:=\mathbb E[I_{12}\mid\sigma(U,V)]=UV/2$ and $\mathbb E J^2=\mathbb E[U^2V^2]/4=h^2/4$. By [F8], $\mathbb E[(I_{12}-J)J]=0$; expanding the square therefore gives $\mathbb E|I_{12}-J|^2=\mathbb E I_{12}^2-\mathbb E J^2=h^2/4>0$. If $I_{12}$ were a measurable function of $(U,V)$, the conditional-expectation identity [F5] would give $I_{12}=J$ almost surely, contradicting this positive residual. Thus the endpoint increments do not determine the required area sample, and any approximation has a separate error and cost. [F1, F3, F4, F5, F8, step 1.3, A1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** Countable Choice; $H,V,J,a$ and $\lambda_j$ as defined above;
$E=\operatorname{span}\{e_1,e_2\}$; and $V_h=E$ for each $h$.

[F1] A bounded Hermitian coercive form on a Hilbert space induces the energy
inner product, and a compact injective dense inclusion gives the compact
coercive-form spectrum ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]],
[[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[thm-compact-coercive-form-spectrum-and-minmax]]).

[F2] The directed energy best-approximation gap is the supremum of normalized
distances to the trial space ([[def-eigenspace-best-approximation-gap]]).

[F3] For an isolated repeated cluster, the conforming Galerkin theorem
compares the invariant eigenspaces and does not select individual eigenvectors
([[thm-conforming-galerkin-eigenspace-gap-under-isolated-cluster]]).

[F4] Under Countable Choice, a complete totally bounded metric space is
compact; the compact-operator definition reduces compactness to compactness of
the closure of a unit-ball image
([[def-totally-bounded]],

Since $\lambda_j\ge1$, $a(u,u)\ge\|Ju\|_H^2$, and $a(u,u)=\|u\|_V^2$; hence the form is coercive and bounded. Finite sequences lie in $V$ and are dense in $H$, so $J$ is injective with dense range. [F1, A1, given, algebra]

1.2 Let $B_V:=\{u\in V:\|u\|_V\le1\}$. For any $\varepsilon>0$, choose $N$ so $1/\sqrt{\lambda_{N+1}}<\varepsilon/2$. If $x=Ju$ with $u\in B_V$, then $\sum_{j>N}|x_j|^2=\sum_{j>N}|u_j|^2\le\lambda_{N+1}^{-1}\sum_{j>N}\lambda_j|u_j|^2\le\lambda_{N+1}^{-1}$. The set $C_N:=\{(z_1,\ldots,z_N)\in\mathbb K^N:\sum_{j\le N}\lambda_j|z_j|^2\le1\}$ is closed and bounded in $\mathbb R^N$ (if $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$) or $\mathbb R^{2N}$ (if $\mathbb K=\mathbb C$), so it is compact by Heine--Borel and has a finite $\varepsilon/2$-net with centers in $C_N$. Each center $z$ lifts by zero padding to $\widetilde z=(z_1,\ldots,z_N,0,\ldots)\in J(B_V)$, because its weighted energy is at most one. For $x=Ju\in J(B_V)$, the prefix $(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$ belongs to $C_N$; the net and the tail bound therefore give $\|x-\widetilde z\|_{\ell^2}<\varepsilon$ for one of these finitely many lifts. Thus $J(B_V)$ is totally bounded with centers in itself. Its closure $C:=\overline{J(B_V)}$ is also totally bounded: a finite $\varepsilon/2$-net for $J(B_V)$ is an $\varepsilon$-net for $C$ by the triangle inequality and the definition of closure. The set $C$ is complete because it is closed in the complete Hilbert space $H$: every Cauchy sequence in $C$ converges in $H$, and closedness keeps its limit in $C$. By [F4], $C$ is compact. The unit-ball criterion in [[def-compact-linear-operator]] now shows that $J$ is compact. [F4, F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Each coordinate vector $e_j$ satisfies $a(e_j,v)=\lambda_j(Je_j,Jv)_H$. For any nonzero $u\in V$, $\frac{a(u,u)}{\|Ju\|_H^2} =\frac{\sum_j\lambda_j|u_j|^2}{\sum_j|u_j|^2}\ge1,$ with equality exactly when $u_j=0$ for all $j\ge3$. Therefore the first eigenvalue is $1$, its full eigenspace is $E$, and the next eigenvalue is $3$. [F1, step 1.2, given, algebra]

3.1 The restriction of the continuous form to $V_h=E$ is the identity form, so both Ritz values are $1$ and the full cluster eigenspace is $E_h=E$. For every $u\in E$, $u\in V_h$, so the definition [F2] gives $\delta_a(E,V_h)=0$; likewise the gap from $E$ to $E_h$ is zero. The cluster theorem [F3] therefore applies with $r=1,s=2$ and its gap conclusion is attained exactly. [F2, F3, step 2.1, given]

4.1 For each $h$, choose $u_h=e_1$ when $h$ is an even positive integer and $u_h=e_2$ when $h$ is odd. Both are unit Ritz eigenvectors for the same repeated eigenvalue $1$. Their successive energy distances are $\|e_1-e_2\|_a=\sqrt2$, so $(u_h)$ is not Cauchy and cannot converge. This does not contradict step 3.1: the invariant subspace remains exactly $E$, while the repeated eigenspace supplies no preferred basis vector. [step 3.1, given, algebra] ∎
